questions.question_text: A speculator buys 50 acres in Vermont, subdivides it, and sells the lots 18 months later at a large profit. Which Vermont tax is aimed squarely at this?
questions.explanation: Vermont's land gains tax (32 V.S.A. ch. 236) reaches gains from the sale of Vermont land that the transferor both purchased and subdivided within six years before the sale. Since Act 175 (H.541, effective January 1, 2020) narrowed the definition of 'land,' land that was NOT subdivided by the transferor is outside the tax no matter how briefly it was held.

questions.question_text: A developer subdivides Vermont farmland and sells parcels after holding the land for 3 years. The land gains tax applies to gains on which portion of the property?
questions.explanation: The land gains tax reaches the gain attributable to the land itself; buildings and other improvements are excluded from the computation (32 V.S.A. § 10002). The tax also only applies if the transferor purchased and subdivided the land within six years of the sale.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is EXEMPT from Vermont's land gains tax?
questions.correct_answer: Land with a dwelling the buyer will occupy as a principal residence, up to 10 acres
distractors: Any commercial lot held more than 4 years
Any parcel a seller inherited rather than purchased at auction
Subdivided farmland held less than 5 years
questions.explanation: The transferee's principal residence exemption covers a dwelling plus up to 10 acres that the transferee will occupy as a domiciled principal residence within one year of purchase (or, on vacant land, will build on and occupy within two years). Other exclusions include certain affordable-housing transfers and agricultural land a farmer transfers to a family member who continues agricultural use so the combined use reaches six years.

questions.question_text: Vermont's land gains tax rates range from 5% up to what maximum percentage based on gain ratio and holding period?
questions.explanation: The rate table in 32 V.S.A. § 10003 runs from 5% (gain under 100% of basis, land held 5 to 6 years) to 80% (gain of 200% or more, land held less than 4 months). A single flat rate applies to the entire gain, determined by the holding period and the gain as a percentage of basis.

questions.question_text: A developer transfers subdivided Vermont land to her adult daughter at fair market value 3 years after buying it. How does the land gains tax apply?
questions.correct_answer: It applies — there is no general family-transfer exemption
distractors: It is exempt as a transfer to a family member
Tax is deferred until the daughter resells
Only 50% of the gain is taxable
questions.explanation: Vermont's land gains tax has no general family exemption. The only family-related exclusion is narrow: agricultural land transferred by a farmer to a member of the farmer's family, where the transferee's agricultural use added to the transferor's equals or exceeds six years. A developer selling subdivided lots to an adult child at market value is a taxable transfer.

questions.question_text: A nonresident sells Vermont property for $400,000. How much must the buyer withhold under Vermont's real estate withholding rules?
distractors: Nothing — withholding applies only to commercial property
questions.explanation: Under 32 V.S.A. § 5847 the buyer must withhold 2.5% of the total sale price when the seller is a nonresident of Vermont — a flat percentage of the price, not a calculation on the gain. 2.5% of $400,000 is $10,000. A seller who expects to owe less can apply for a Commissioner's Certificate before closing to reduce or eliminate the withholding.

questions.question_text: Which form must a buyer file within 30 days of transferring Vermont property from a nonresident seller?
questions.explanation: The buyer files Form RW-171 with payment within 30 days of the transfer, unless the seller has obtained a Commissioner's Certificate exempting the transaction. The withholding is a prepayment of the seller's Vermont income tax, not a separate tax.

questions.question_text: A nonresident seller completing a Section 1031 exchange wants to reduce the Vermont withholding requirement. What document should the seller obtain?
questions.explanation: A Commissioner's Certificate from the Vermont Commissioner of Taxes, obtained before closing, may reduce or eliminate the 2.5% withholding when the seller's actual Vermont tax liability will be lower — for example under a federal §121 principal residence exclusion or a §1031 like-kind exchange.

questions.question_text: After Vermont real estate withholding is collected from a nonresident's sale, on which form does the seller claim credit for the amount withheld?
questions.explanation: The nonresident seller claims credit for the amount withheld on their Vermont income tax return, Form IN-111. The withholding serves as a prepayment of the seller's Vermont income tax liability.

questions.question_text: A Vermont buyer purchases from a nonresident seller for $300,000. The seller's capital gain is $80,000. What must the buyer withhold?
questions.explanation: Vermont's nonresident withholding is 2.5% of the sale price under 32 V.S.A. § 5847, regardless of the size of the seller's gain: 2.5% of $300,000 is $7,500. The seller's actual tax is settled on the Vermont return (Form IN-111), where the withheld amount is claimed as a credit; a Commissioner's Certificate obtained before closing is the way to reduce withholding up front.

questions.question_text: In many Vermont municipalities, which fiscal year is used for property tax proration at closing?
questions.explanation: Many Vermont municipalities operate on a July 1 through June 30 fiscal year for property tax purposes. This must be considered when prorating taxes between buyer and seller at closing.

questions.question_text: At a Vermont closing, which two types of property taxes are typically prorated separately between buyer and seller?
questions.explanation: Vermont property tax bills combine a statewide education property tax with the municipal (town) tax, and the two are commonly prorated separately at closing because the rates and billing cycles differ. The proration method is a contract term, set in the purchase and sale agreement.

questions.question_text: A Vermont purchase agreement closes August 15 with a July 1 fiscal year. The seller has NOT yet paid the current year taxes. Who owes the prorated share for July 1 through August 14?
questions.correct_answer: The seller owes a credit to the buyer
distractors: The buyer owes a credit to the seller
Each party pays their own share directly
The title company retains the full amount
questions.explanation: Since the seller occupied the property from July 1 through August 14 but hasn't paid taxes, the seller owes the buyer a credit at closing for those 45 days of prorated property taxes.

questions.question_text: Where is the method of property tax proration for a Vermont real estate transaction typically specified?
questions.explanation: The proration method for property taxes is specified in the purchase agreement between buyer and seller. This ensures both parties agree in advance on how taxes will be divided at closing.

questions.question_text: A Vermont closing occurs on October 1. Annual municipal tax is $3,600 on a July 1 fiscal year, and the seller has already paid in full. How much does the buyer owe the seller?
questions.explanation: The seller prepaid the full $3,600. From October 1 through June 30 is 9 months. The buyer owes the seller 9/12 of $3,600, which equals $2,700 as a credit to the seller at closing.
